messages.subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manushi,

In general, a few of the tools that NIMBLE provides to help with this are:

1) trying different samplers for one or more nodes (e.g., switching
from random walk Metropolis ("RW") samplers to slice samplers or using
the RW sampler on the log scale). See Sec 7.2 of the NIMBLE manual.
2) if the node (i.e. ,parameter) is highly correlated with one or more
other nodes, blocking nodes together, e.g., with the RW_block sampler.
There's a bit of an example
in Section 2.6 of the manual or see the "Customizing an MCMC" and
"Building a generalized linear mixed model" examples at
https://r-nimble.org/examples.
3) writing your own customized sampler (if you have some idea of how
to make better proposals for the slow-mixing parameter). See Sec 15.5
of the manual.
4) In some cases, finding better starting values for the MCMC can help.
5) Sometimes reparameterizing the model helps, though that is not
explicitly something that is part of NIMBLE.

Other users might weigh in with strategies that they've used.

messages.subject: Re: Improving MCMC convergence
messages.body_plain:
I'll add some strategies to what Chris wrote.

Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z).  Sometimes changing the parameterization of a model (e.g. from non-centered to centered random effects) or centering explanatory variables can lead to improved mixing.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Zhihua, I'm not an expert with the use of the dCRP distribution in NIMBLE, but I can say for certain that NIMBLE is expecting a *vector* valued node to be assigned the dCRP prior.  That is, something more like:

  for (j in 1:4) {

       b[1:S, j] ~ CRP(.....)
   }

Or something along those lines.

Although, for getting to the bottom of this, a full example of the model you're trying to create, ideally in a fully reproducible example of the code, would be the most helpful for sure.

Good luck, and keep in touch.

Daniel

messages.subject: NIMBLE version 0.7.1 released
messages.body_plain:
Version 0.7.1 is primarily a maintenance release with a couple important
bug fixes, but also a few new features.

The bug fixes relate to the issues mentioned in previous announcements,
namely (1) a protection stack overflow affecting large models and (2) a bug
affecting MCMC sampling of dCRP nodes in Bayesian nonparametric
models in nonconjugate settings. Users with large models and users of the
dCRP distribution are strongly encouraged to update to version 0.7.1.

New features include:
-- Adding support for 6-dimensional arrays in model code and in nimbleFunctions.
-- Allowing use of besselK in model code.
-- Adding normal-normal conjugacy detection in multivariate regression
structures using inprod, sum, and matrix multiplication.
-- Allowing use of 'x' in addition to 'value' in 'types' argument to
registerDistributions.

Please see the NEWS file in the installed package for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

messages.subject: Re: Spatial random effects with car.normal
messages.body_plain:
Rui, thanks for continuing to correspond with me about the error you were experiencing using the car.normal distribution in NIMBLE.  It was helpful to help diagnose the problem.

After looking into this, I found a minor bug in the NIMBLE's MCMC conjugacy checking system, the specific only for CAR model structure.  Specifically, the conjugacy checking of the individual components of the CAR distribution was giving a situation where the "deterministic node expansion" was resulting in the wrong expanded expression, and thus not finding the CAR node for the conjugacy check, which should always be in that expression.  In this case, your use of car.normal, or equivalently, dcar_normal, for spatial random effects distribution, was triggering the bug.

The good news, is that this bug would only cause some model structures to fail at the time of MCMC building (buildMCMC()), and would never result in an MCMC being built, or giving incorrect results.  So there's no danger of incorrect inferences.

Also, I was able to fix this bug, so that the MCMC will operate fine on these CAR models.  The fix has been added to our development branch ("devel") of NIMBLE.  Until our next release, when this will be added to the version of NIMBLE on CRAN, you can install this development version directly using the R code below.

remove.packages('nimble')
library(devtools)
install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

Please try this out, and let me know if this fixes the problem for your model.

Cheers, thanks for your use of NIMBLE.

Daniel
for the NIMBLE development team

messages.subject: monitor adaptation in block RW
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to the developers and countless contributors for all the great work building this useful software.

Is there a way to monitor the adaptation steps used in NIMBLE's RW and block RW samplers? I am having an issue with a some samplers that get stuck after several thousand iterations, even after specifying thoughtful initial proposal covariances, and I think being able to see the details of the proposal distributions might be helpful.

messages.body_snippet:

Is there a way to monitor the adaptation steps used in NIMBLE's RW and block RW samplers

messages.subject: Re: monitor adaptation in block RW
messages.body_plain:
Yes, there are nice facilities for recording this information built into both NIMBLE's RW and RW_block samplers.  You can "turn these on" by setting the nimble package option:

> nimbleOptions(saveMCMChistory = TRUE)

Then you can retrieve this information, using member methods of the samplers, e.g.:

> Cmcmc$samplerFunctions$contentsList[[i]]$getScaleHistory()
or,
> Cmcmc$samplerFunctions$contentsList[[i]]$getPropCovHistory()

You'll need to replace "i" with the correct sampler number, in the lines above.  To see what methods are available, I'd suggest looking at the source code for, for example, the RW_block sampler, available here:

https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R

Great question!  Keep in touch.

Daniel

Hi Alison,

On Fri, Mar 29, 2019 at 8:49 AM Alison Ketz <aliso...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you all so much for your hard work and development of this software. In this post I'm making a feature request and asking a few questions
>
> I'm running several large models with loads of data, and would like to compare these models using WAIC.
> Using thin/thin2 I've been able to obtain WAIC values on a simple model. Unfortunately, with more complex models, WAIC returns as NaN with the suggestion of tracing latent states. If I do trace latent states, this will break down when nimble tries to return the latent state nodes because this array is too large for R. Would it be possible to trace latent states for the purpose of computing WAIC within c++, without having that object returned to R (since that's where it breaks). The models compile and run otherwise. Is WAIC computed prior to thinning? Is it computed using the minimum size if thin/thin2 are different?
>

First, some preliminaries: Are you up to date on nimble?  There was a bug fix a couple of versions or so back in which WAIC could fail when combining multiple chains.  If that is the source of your NaN, it might be resolved simply by updating nimble.

No, the WAIC does not currently work just within C++.

WAIC should be post-thinning.  No, there is not a clever combination of thin and thin2.  WAIC is calculated from the monitors with thin, not the monitors2 with thin2.  I think you could make the more highly thinned case be monitors and thin, with everything you need for WAIC.  If you want a less thinned sample without latent states, you could do that in monitors2 and thin2.

> Also, because of the size of both the models and data, ideally we'd run them with parallel chains. This brings up a few questions:
> 1. If we do run the chains in parallel, seems like we won't be able to compute WAIC using all samples from all chains, similar to how the nimbleMCMC function does, unless we do it manually (feature request implied)

That is correct.  You could do the following: After running chains in parallel (see below), append samples from all chains into the mvSamples of one of the Cmcmc objects.  Then, call its calculateWAIC method.  To append the chains together, first append them in an R matrix, using for example rbind.  Then do nimble:::matrix2mv(posteriorSamplesMatrix, Cmcmc$mvSamples), where posteriorSamplesMatrix is the matrix of combined samples. This will copy posteriorSamplesMatrix into Cmcmc$mvSamples, from which WAIC is calculated.  See source code for runMCMC for an example of this maneuver.  The "nimble:::" is necessary because matrix2mv is not an exported package function because there hasn't been a use case like this before, but maybe it should be.

> 2. I've seen on other posts that we need to compile the model and mcmc seperately. Does this include building and configuring the mcmc? I have gotten it to run and return samples with just compiling the mcmc. However, when returning the compiled/run object, i.e. Cmcmc, this causes R to segfault and crash. I've gotten a few error messages including:

Yes, you need to start with a new model object and a new MCMC object in each thread and compile them in each thread. (Actually, they can be compiled in a single call to compileNimble, which will return a list, but I think people typically do them in two calls.  But that's not really the nub of your question.) The errors you report could come from not doing so.  From what you did, the multiple compiled MCMCs may have run and returned samples, but they would have been using the same compiled model object, creating mayhem and results that should not be trusted, as well as the kind of crash you report.  Improving capability to parallelize is a big design goal but one that will take some time.

There is one step of the process where you can save processing.  Once you have an uncompiled model object, say Rmodel, then Rmodel$newModel(replicate=TRUE) should return a new model object with all the same content as the old one.  As always, using check=FALSE (may be default) and calculate=FALSE will save some time.

I hope it all helps.  Thanks for the questions.

The core developers are spread out among trips, so further answers may be slower than usual in the next week or two.

-Perry

Hi All,

I'm trying to estimate the parameters of Zero-Inflated Conway Maxwell Poisson distribution in Nimble using MCMC algorithm.

I took reference from the example provided on the Nimble website for Zero-inflated Poisson distribution.

I was expecting the same behavior of the algorithm as in Zero-Inflated Poisson example, But I don't why it is behaving so weirdly,

Can somebody please help me out in this situation.

library(CompGLM)
library(nimble)

ZICMPcode <- nimbleCode({
  p~dunif(0,1)
  lam~dunif(0,100)
  nu~dunif(0,100)
  for(i in 1:N) {
    y[i] ~ dZICMP(lam, nu,sumTo = 200L,zeroProb = p)
  }

} )

## constants, data, and initial values
constants <- list(N = 100)

dCMP <- nimbleRcall(function(y = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(),logP = logical(0, default = 0)){}, Rfun = 'dcomp',
                    returnType = double(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

rCMP <- nimbleRcall(function(n = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer()){}, Rfun = 'rcomp',
                    returnType = integer(), envir = .GlobalEnv)

dZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double())
    ## First handle non-zero data
    if(x != 0) {
      ## return the log probability if log = TRUE
      if(log) return(dCMP(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = TRUE) + log(1-zeroProb))
      ## or the probability if log = FALSE
      else return((1-zeroProb) * dCMP(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE))
    }
    ## From here down we know x is 0
    totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1-zeroProb) * dCMP(0, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE)
    if(log) return(log(totalProbZero))
    return(totalProbZero)
  })

rZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double()) {
    returnType(integer())
    isStructuralZero <- rbinom(1, prob = zeroProb, size = 1)
    if(isStructuralZero) return(0)
    return(rCMP(1, lam,nu,sumTo = 200L))
  })

registerDistributions(list(
  dZICMP = list(
    BUGSdist = "dZICMP(lam, nu,sumTo, zeroProb)",
    discrete = TRUE,
    range = c(0, Inf),
    types = c('value = integer()', 'lam = double()', 'nu = double()','sumTo = integer()', 'zeroProb = double()')
  )))

ZICMPmodel <- nimbleModel( ZICMPcode,constants=constants,check = FALSE)

ZICMPmodel$p <- .4
ZICMPmodel$lam <- 1.8
ZICMPmodel$nu<-0.9
ZICMPmodel$simulate('y')
simulatedData <- ZICMPmodel$y
simulatedData
hist(simulatedData)

ZICMPmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedData))
cZICMPmodel <- compileNimble(ZICMPmodel)
ZICMPmcmc <- buildMCMC(ZICMPmodel)
cZICMPmcmc <- compileNimble(ZICMPmcmc, project = ZICMPmodel)
cZICMPmcmc$run(10000)
samples <- as.matrix(cZICMPmcmc$mvSamples)
summary(samples)
plot(samples[,'lam'], main = 'lambda trace plot')
plot(samples[,'nu'], main = 'nu trace plot')
plot(samples[,'p'], main = 'zeroProb trace plot')
